analysis.one_liner: Redirects tariff revenue from a US-EU beef trade dispute to grants for US beef producers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Agriculture Committee after one subcommittee hearing on September 25, 2000, and expired when the 106th Congress ended January 3, 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The US won a World Trade Organization case over the European Union's ban on American hormone-treated beef, and the US responded by putting extra tariffs on European products. This bill would sweep that tariff money into a new Treasury trust fund earmarked for the beef industry, handed out as grants to a beef promotion and research board to improve beef quality and market American beef overseas. The fund would end only if the EU lifted its ban. The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, got one subcommittee hearing, and never moved further.
analysis.who_benefits: US beef producers, particularly ranchers who say they lost European sales because of the EU's ban on hormone-treated beef. Grants would flow through a federally recognized beef promotion and research board to improve beef quality and promote US beef in overseas markets [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: US cattle ranchers and beef promoters

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Beef Industry Compensation Trust Fund in the Treasury, funded by amounts equal to the extra duties collected on European Union products on the US beef retaliation list [S2][S3].
Authorizes the Agriculture Secretary to grant fund money to a nationally recognized beef promotion and research board to help US producers improve beef quality and develop overseas markets [S2][S3].
Terminates the fund only when the EU complies with the WTO ruling allowing US beef producers access to the European market and the retaliation duties stop [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury and taxpayers, who lose the retaliation-duty revenue that would otherwise go to the general fund, and consumers who already pay the inflated prices on European goods hit by the retaliatory tariffs (such as specialty foods on the retaliation list) [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and buyers of tariffed EU goods

drawbacks.text: It earmarks tariff revenue for one commodity group: money collected at the border that would ordinarily go into the general Treasury would instead fund promotion and research for a single industry [S2][S3].
Retaliatory tariffs raise prices for American consumers on the targeted European imports, and the bill gives them nothing in return while routing that revenue to beef producers [S3].

The termination trigger is EU compliance, which the EU had refused to provide for years over the hormone-beef dispute, so the fund could persist indefinitely without a sunset date independent of EU behavior [S2][S3].
Grants flow through the government-recognized beef checkoff promotion and research board, building on an existing industry-run promotion structure rather than creating independent oversight [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives a targeted, plausible remedy to producers hurt by a real trade injury, but it does so by diverting public tariff revenue to one industry and leaves consumers of the tariffed European goods worse off. The cost is modest in dollar terms, but the design sets a precedent for turning trade-retaliation money into sector-specific subsidies.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced, got a single subcommittee hearing in September 2000, and died there when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Max Baucus introduced the bill on June 8, 2000, joined by five other senators as original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S1][S3][S5].
The committee's Subcommittee on Forestry, Conservation, and Rural Revitalization held a hearing on September 25, 2000, with a printed hearing record [S5].
The full committee never reported the bill, and no Senate or House vote ever occurred before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers and the Treasury kept the retaliation-duty revenue in the general fund; the beef industry gained nothing because the compensation fund was never created.

for.name: Sen. Max Baucus
for.role: Lead sponsor; senior member and former ranking member of the Senate Agriculture Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor on June 8, 2000 [S1][S3][S5].

for.name: Sens. Kit Bond, Jeff Bingaman, Byron Dorgan, Tom Daschle, and Bob Kerrey
for.role: Original cosponsors spanning both parties, including the Senate Democratic leader
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced [S3].

for.name: 9 cosponsors (4 Republicans, 5 Democrats)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support from the start [S4].

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Richard Lugar (R-IN)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee for one hearing, then never reported it to the full Senate; no markup or committee vote appears in the action history [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship from day one — nine cosponsors split 4 Republicans and 5 Democrats, with the Democratic leader among them — and the record shows no opposition vote; it simply died unreported in committee [S4][S5].

industries.industry: US beef producers and cattle ranchers
industries.note: They would receive dedicated tariff revenue as grants for quality improvement and overseas promotion, compensating for lost EU sales caused by the hormone-beef ban. The money comes from public tariff receipts rather than from the EU, so the gain is partly at taxpayers' expense.

industries.industry: Beef checkoff promotion and research boards
industries.note: The bill routes all compensation through the nationally recognized beef promotion and research board, locking in that industry-run board as the permanent channel for the new public money.

industries.industry: Importers and sellers of tariffed European goods (specialty foods, mustard, Roquefort and similar items on the retaliation list)
industries.note: They already pay the 100% retaliatory duties, which raise prices for their customers; the bill keeps those duties in place and directs the revenue away from the general Treasury. The bill does not change the duties themselves.
